Rumour has it that members of that commission will include the Hon. Donald Macdonald, one of the architects of the problem in the first place, and Ian Stewart, the right hand man and the fall-guy for the whole massive failure, the Hon. At least it should be spared the embarrassment of having its own policies called into question. Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That the Government, following the same sort of reasoning as the foregoing, encourage municipalities across the country to appoint to their police commissions only practising criminals and to appoint only known polluters to probe environmental hazards.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. A year ago I asked the Government, when the unemployment rate was at 8.3 per cent, what it would do to stimulate employment. At that time I was advised by the Government that I should await the budget of the Minister of Finance in that November because it would contain initiatives to stimulate employment. History has shown us that, not only did it not create any employment initiatives, indeed the budget was instrumental in causing the historic high unemployment rates which we have this morning.
Last week the new Minister of Finance announced a job creation program which would create 60,000 jobs. In light of this morning's statistics on unemployment levels in the country, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance what changes he is considering to his statement of last week.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, indeed the figures released this morning are very distressing. However, I remind the Hon. Member that in my statement of last week I indicated that we should expect such high levels of unemployment over the next while, that unemployment will only gradually decline over next year, 1983, and that we should take all necessary steps to help those most in need during that particular period. Although the economy will know

November 5, 1982
Oral Questions
recovery during 1983, the impact on unemployment will only be slow and gradual.
I remind the Hon. Member that, contrary to his initial statement, a number of measures were contained in both the November and the June budgets to help create jobs. As a matter of fact, we allocated SI.2 billion in job creation programs during that period. On top of this 1 announced last week a $1.1 billion program of direct and indirect job creation which should contribute toward alleviating this particular problem. However, 1 also indicated that we were under no illusion that this would have a dramatic impact on the unemployment level. That will only take place with a general recovery and with a resurgence of activity both in Canada and internationally. I remind the Hon. Member that unemployment at the present time is high in all industrialized countries by historical standards, and that we will pursue very actively our program of economic recovery.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: I take it from the response that the Minister is saying that there will not be any change in the Government's program in light of the statistics this morning.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister who speaks for the Minister of State for Social Development in the other place, I will direct my next question to the Minister of Finance. The major thrust of the program of the Minister of Finance as stated last week was the creation of 60,000 jobs primarily aimed for those coming off unemployment insurance.
I am sure the Minister of Finance is aware that the unemployment level this morning for people between the ages of 15 and 24, the majority of whom are not the so-called exhaustees of unemployment insurance, stands at 21 per cent. I would like to ask the Minister if he has any specific program to help these people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 would like to point out to the Hon. Member that we do in fact have a number of programs that are directed to helping young people get first-time employment in the job market. The Canada Community Development Projects, as I have said in the House before, are now coming onstream and will provide, between now and Christmas, close to 60,000 new jobs. About 40 per cent of those jobs will go to people under the age of 24 in terms of direct employment.
We introduced a program last summer whereby we provide a subsidy of up to $2 an hour to employers under the Program for the Employment Disadvantaged in order to attract young people into the job market and give them first-time job experience.
We have those two programs in place, as well as a number of others related to student employment, and a new Outreach Program which provides proper counselling and guidance for young people so that they can go into the training programs which we are also introducing this year. We really have a three-pronged approach to try to address the problems of young people. We recognize it to be one of the very serious pressure points in the over-all employment picture.
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has the same position as the Minister of Finance, and that is not to make any changes in light of the statistics this morning.

subsubtopic: RETENTION OF FOREIGN WORKERS BY ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I would like to get down to some specifics. Does the Minister know that Atomic Energy is laying off qualified Canadians while at the same time keeping foreigners on work permits on staff? May I ask the Minister if he will investigate this matter as it does not do much to encourage Canadians to trust this administration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: RETENTION OF FOREIGN WORKERS BY ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 am always prepared to investigate any matter that is brought forward by a Member of Parliament. The Hon. Member, being an immigration critic in this House, should know full well that we have established a very firm policy. As far as employment is concerned, the first choice and opportunity for any job goes to a Canadian. We do not authorize any employment or immigration visa until an employer has tested right across Canada to see if there is an available Canadian for the job. In fact, when the immigration levels were established just last week, we put a total restriction on workers from overseas to ensure that Canadian workers have the first chance. This demonstrates that we are giving encouragement to Canadians to get those jobs first.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Unemployment today is up again at 1.4 million. This is the same level as for fully one-half of the years of the Great Depression. The response of the Government seems to be to appoint a commission of inquiry into economic matters. How can the Minister justify the appointment of the same people who got us into this economic mess, as a substitute for real economic strategy?

November 5, 1982

Madam Speaker, obviously, I have no comment to make on the speculation to which the Hon. Member refers, but I will refer him to the fact that, for 12 weeks in a row now, we have seen a decline in the bank rate. We have also seen a decline in the inflation rate. Which will lead, as it has led in the past, to lower interest rates. It will help stimulate business in this country, it will help the people with mortgages, and it will help the construction industry. I remind him that the housing industry association is now predicting some 150,000 housing starts next year, compared to much lower rates this year. So there are hopeful times on the horizon. The oil and gas industry has forecast a very good year in 1983. Some even predict it will be a better year in 1983 than the record year in 1980.
My consultations in the United States indicate that investment houses there, for instance, foresee a better year for Canadian oil and gas in 1983 than in the U.S.
The Hon. Member asks about unemployment. Indeed, this is going to create jobs for Canadians. If the oil and gas industry, and the housing industry keep on, as is being forecast by the industries themselves, that is going to create jobs. We are going to generate jobs by lower interest rates and more activity in the private sector. That is what we need, jobs of a permanent nature. We will do our best as a Government to help those who are in need, and to create temporary jobs to ease us over this extremely difficult period. But things are happening at the present time which are encouraging.

Madam Speaker, the Minister seems to describe as signs of recovery those which are indicators of the recession. An official of the Department of Employment has indicated that half the jobs lost over the last year are gone forever, yet the Government's response in the Minister's economic statement has been the NEED Program which will simply recycle people back into the unemployment insurance system after 20 weeks of work, while Unemployment Insurance Premiums go up, which is a drag on the economy. When is the Minister going to adopt an economic strategy which really works for people, rather than continuing to dampen the economy?

Madam Speaker, I covered that quite extensively in my statement of last week and I invite my hon. friend to read it if he did not listen to it at that time. I indicated at that time there were a number of measures the Government could take, and was taking, to help those most in need in this difficult time, but the thrust of my economic statement and the thrust of the economic policy of this Government is to create the environment whereby the private sector is going to be the engine of the recovery. This is what we have been working on ever since my predecessor introduced the six and five program on June 28 of this year.
I wish the Hon. Member's party would support that program because it has produced very good effects-
More unemployment.

-and it will produce even better effects. As far as the broad issue is concerned, I remind my hon. friend that, even in the United States, and in Europe at the present time they are also experiencing a recession. There are 30 million unemployed in the OECD countries at the present time. We are part of this very difficult world we are living in, and we will do everything we can to make sure that Canada is not going to suffer as much as it could otherwise.

Madam Speaker, I wonder how the Minister can justify a Canada which has become a nation of part-time workers, a Canada in which we have lost 500,000 permanent jobs, a Canada in which job creation means 20 weeks of work to requalify for unemployment insurance-when people need permanent full-time work? How can Canadians trust a Government that acts like that?
[ Translation]

Madam Speaker, we are not trying to justify the situation but to correct it. That is the government's role, and that is what we are trying to do. We are trying to use all the resources at our disposal and those we can develop with the private sector, labour and management and the provincial governments, so that Canada will experience the economic recovery we all need. My hon. colleague should realize, however, that the present world situation is such that even the United States is experiencing the highest level of unemployment it has ever known. So that is the situation, and we will all have to make a joint effort to create an economic environment that will provide the necessary stimulation, instead of merely criticizing as the Hon. Member is doing.

November 5, 1982

Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is a very good investigator. It is public knowledge that well over a year ago, we were about to see the first stage of a merger between Nordair and Quebecair. At that time, the Quebec government intervened to prevent this, for political reasons, and invested $15 million in Quebecair which it considered a commercially viable operation, an investment which today does not have the same value as it did at the time. Now, the Quebec Minister of Transport is trying to blame us for the decision it made then, and the telegram he sent us today should be seen in that light. The fact is that there is no fundamental difference between Section 15(1) of the Aeronautics Act, which goes back to 1977 and prohibits transfer of control of an air carrier to a provincial government, and Bill S-31, which prohibits a provincial government from holding more than 10 per cent of the shares of an air or other carrier. There is no basic difference between the two sets of legislation.

I do not think it is fair to say the problem is getting out of hand or that it is worse than it has been in the past. In fact we have learned a great deal from hostage-taking incidents, and I think we have done a lot to avoid some of the past causes of hostage-taking incidents.

November 5, 1982

rules-what are the parameters of the investigators, whoever they may be? I assume that people within the Minister's Department are looking into this. Madam Speaker, two types of investigation are virtually automatic. In the first case the police are called in because crimes or offences have been committed. I would remind the House that a hostage taking is a violation of the Criminal Code. The police come in and they are completely independent from the Government, from the system and from the correctional service. They have full access to everyone, and they lay charges when charges are justified. They also make recommendations when those are justified.
The second string is the work of the Inspector General. The purpose of his investigation is not to find fault with anyone- that is left to the police-the purpose of his investigation is to make recommendations for dealing with the type of situation that gave rise to a particular hostage taking. In order to be effective, confidentiality applies to the work and the report of the Inspector General. I will be prepared to make a statement when I have the report of the Inspector General on the Stony Mountain incident. I can assure the Hon. Member that, where action is justified and can be taken to reassure the surrounding community, which is the most important thing, to reassure the members of the staff, even to reassure the inmates about their personal safety and security in the face of the violence that caused these incidents, then I will be prepared to make a statement about it.

subsubtopic: RCMP POLICY REGARDING PAYMENT TO WITNESSES
speechtext:
1. (a) Witnesses called by the Crown in criminal cases are entitled to fees and expenses in accordance with the tariffs set by provincial laws or regulations. See also payments to informers in part 2 below. RCMP policy provides for compliance with the schedules and tariffs including Section 772 of the Criminal Code to facilitate these payments.
(b) No, the general policy does not involve payments beyond expenses incurred in connection with court appearances. There is, however, additional policy which deals specifically with the Force's Witness Protection Program and is separate from those witness entitlements provided for by provincial laws or regulations. Payments made in this Program pertain only to relocation and cost of living expenses for a witness and family should the life of the witness or his/her family become endangered as a result of co-operation with the Crown or agreement to testify. The payment of moneys or benefits are not authorized to any person simply in return for their testimony.
2.	Yes, there is RCMP policy concerning payments to informers. This policy deals with the following:
(a)	the amount of payments: These payments are authorized at varying levels of authority within the RCMP in accordance with Treasury Board directives;
(b)	the criteria for payments: In each case the criteria for payment is established by the levels of authority responsible for authorizing payment. They must be satisfied that the expenses are fair and just in relation to the assistance rendered or information received:
(c)	the selection of recipients: Not all informants or witnesses receive payments. Payments occur only in those circumstances which dictate the need.
In the event of a paid informer being a witness, Force practice requires, without exception, full disclosure of all details to the Court.
In Security Service matters, it is not in the interests of maintaining internal security to make public policy concerning payments to informers.

That this House condemns the government for their incompetent management of the unemployment insurance system and their mishandling and misdirection of employment programs:
(a)	by creating and tolerating long and unconscionable delays in payment of earned benefits to claimants;
(b)	by refusing to provide extended benefits or jobs to the growing thousands of unemployed whose benefits are expiring each month;
(c)	by raising unemployment insurance premiums by 40 to 53% at a time when U1C services are declining and in disrepute; and
Supply
finally, condemns the government for fumbling a growing myriad of uncoordinated hit and miss job creation programs and its consequent failure to begin to provide some meaningful employment and stable incomes for over 1.4 million jobless Canadians.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is very important that the House of Commons begin to deal with the whole question involving the unemployment insurance system and people who are in desperate need of employment. There has been a complete lack of economic policy by the Government of the day. Today the unemployment insurance statistics indicate a new record of unemployment since the great depression. I want to put some of those statistics on the record so that people will be aware of exactly what we mean when we say that unemployment is at the highest level since the depression.
This is the fourteenth consecutive month of decline in jobs. Over the last month we lost another 24,000 jobs and we have lost half a million jobs since October last year. Of the jobs which have disappeared over the last month, 48,000 were full-time jobs. Many people have been forced into part-time employment, which tends artificially to keep the numbers up.
The decline in jobs has been widespread. It has gone through the manufacturing sector, which experienced a loss of
25,000	jobs over the last month, and through the construction sector, with losses amounting to 17,000 jobs over the last month. In light of the comments of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) during question period today that somehow the drop in interest rates which is taking place is an indicator of future recovery, I would respond by saying the drop is the result of such a deep and long lasting recession. He claimed that the drop in interest rates would stimulate construction, but that clearly is not evident from the statistics which show that we have lost some 17,000 jobs in construction over the last month and another 15,000 jobs in trades. Unemployment continues at record levels without abatement.
It is very important to consider exactly what that means. While we might carry on some debate over whether to describe the situation as a recession or a depression, I think that all could agree that what we are living through and what we have been living through over the last year is clearly an economic crisis in the order of the last great depression. Therefore, 1 would call this recession "the great recession". It is long lasting, it is fundamental and it is hurting Canadian people like no other economic crisis has hurt the Canadian people since the great depression.
Today the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had the nerve to stand up in the House of Commons, in response to what appeared to be a set-up question from a backbencher, to announce the creation of a royal commission. We know that in 1949 and 1953 the Liberal Party went the route of a royal commission in order to try to save its political skin. We know that a former member of the Liberal Party became involved in one of these commissions and eventually became Minister of Finance. Therefore, a royal commission which is to study the economy over the next year, shall we say-but who knows- will obviously be an excuse for lack of action. More than that, I suspect it may be a mechanism for political succession. The gentleman who has been appointed to head this royal commis-

November 5, 1982
Supply
sion which, ostensibly, should be independent, one Mr. Macdonald, has been mentioned by some as an aspiring leadership candidate for the Liberal Party when the Prime Minister finally steps down. I just wonder whether this is not a platform enabling him to go across the country to hear people's opinions on the economy so that he can be in line, in first place in succession, when the time comes. I suspect the Government's response to unemployment and to the economic crisis is more political than economic. Indeed, that is shameful and regretful.
The great depression brought about some fundamental political, social and economic change. It moved the North American economy from a laissez-faire attitude to an economic approach to management of the economy which involved activism on the part of government. It involved direct intervention of government into the economy and established social welfare programs which are still with us today and are constantly under threat. The last economic crisis led to some fundamental social and economic change, to some innovation, and eventually to an economic recovery.
What is lacking in the present economic crisis, this great recession, is fundamental innovation in the economic area. This is really what must take place if we are to respond in a realistic manner to the shocking unemployment which exists in Canada today.
We must display courage and move beyond the simple use of fiscal and monetary policies to some measure of setting national economic goals. The only way that we in the country will be able to pull together in order to provide employment for all who need it and want it is by sitting down together as a nation and setting some national economic goals. The countries in the world which have done best, even in these troubled times, are those that have gone that route. It is time for the Canadian Government and the Canadian people to move beyond a simple reliance upon fiddling with fiscal and monetary policies.
After the innovations of the great depression, the economic solutions of those days were often associated with the name of the economist Keynes. After the recovery and some economic growth many people began to feel somewhat smug. We thought we really knew the answers to all economic problems and that a depression could never occur again. We thought we had the technical answers and the know-how to solve the problems.
Clearly the great depression will not repeat itself, but we have another real economic crisis. It did not just start yesterday or this morning; it has been around for some time. For example, we could date it with the oil embargo of 1974 and with the new economic problems which arose thereafter, problems of rising unemployment at the same time as rising inflation, problems which demonstrated that the economic remedies of the past were just not capable of coping with the economic problems of the country. It is only now that it is becoming clear how deep the economic crisis is and how inadequate the measures of the Canadian Government are to
deal with the crisis. It is time for innovation in economic and social matters.
Rather than innovation Canadians are experiencing a reaction. It is a reaction to the difficult problems and to the inadequacy of governmental response to the problems. Now we have a Government which is totally discredited, which is not doing anything real about employment, which is calling a depressed economy a sign of recovery. In the community there is a reaction to the lack of effective intervention by the Government into the economy. There is a conservative reaction which is often called neo-conservatism.
In his latest economic statement the Minister of Finance adopted the same approach. The reaction to the ineptness of the Government's economic approach has discredited its role and led to the conclusion by many that the way to solve economic problems is to take government out of the economy and leave it to the private sector. We have begun to hear this line not only from the Conservatives' but also from the Liberals in their latest economic statement. They are mirror images of one another. They want to leave economic recovery to the private sector and to the United States. They want to wait for the American economy to recover and hope that we can somehow hitch our wagon to theirs.
Canadians are disillusioned with this failure to come to grips with the real problems facing them. We want a Government which is willing to deal with real problems and find real solutions. Also we want a Government which has the courage to implement, to experiment, to attempt in a humane manner, to meet the needs of all Canadians and to ensure that all Canadians have employment and decent incomes.
I want to examine more closely the economic statement of the Minister of Finance. It has been called an economic statement, but it was clearly a budget. There were enough items in it to indicate that it was a budget. The Minister simply took the opportunity to fly it under another flag. The centrepiece of the economic statement was called the NEED Program. It was a job creation Program. The Government claimed it would allocate some $500 million to create some
60,000	jobs over a period of 18 months. I think from experience we must examine more closely what the Government has had to say, what it claimed it was doing. We have been disillusioned in the past as it has made announcement after announcement and there were no changes in the unemployment statistics. The fact is that we now have close to two million Canadians looking for work.
The rule of thumb with regard to employment creation accepted by most labour analysts, including officials in the Department of Employment, is that $500 million will create some 25,000 full-time, one-year jobs. The Government is talking about creating 25,000 jobs at a time when there are 1.4 million people unemployed according to the statistics.
This is clearly inadequate tokenism. It is even worse than that because the Government does not really intend to create full-time jobs. It appears that what it intends to do is create a series of part-time jobs in co-operation with the Provinces which will provide a revolving door between unemployment
November 5, 1982

insurance, short-term work of 20 weeks, for example, and then back to unemployment insurance. This is a very cruel and callous approach to unemployment. It is not a real solution, yet it is the centrepiece of the Government's job creation plan. The provincial Government of Quebec has already put in place a program which would employ people for a period of 20 weeks. The clear intention of such a program is to requalify people for unemployment insurance so that they can pass through the revolving door. The problem with the revolving door is that it is very difficult on the persons who have to live this way. We all know that they need full-time, permanent jobs.
The centrepiece of the Government's job creation Program in its economic statement is a part-time job creation plan which will create a revolving door between unemployment insurance and part-time or short-term work. That is not good enough, it is cruel, and it is insensitive.
I want to refer briefly to some of the other job creation items mentioned in the economic statement so as not to let them go without comment. In the statement $400 million is mentioned for railway investment and development. The statement also indicates that this investment is tied to the resolution of the Crowsnest Pass rate issue. That issue is not resolved, so that money is not moving. If that investment is tied to the resolution of the Crowsnest Pass rate, what the Government is doing is taking money out of the pockets of the farmers and putting it into the pocket of the railway companies. That will not create employment.
We know from past experience that when you invest in railways, you do not have more jobs but a loss of jobs. It has been a question of job loss rather than investment in railways resulting in job creation. We should be skeptical of investment in railways.
Another part of the economic statement as it relates to job creation is the question of where to find the money, from where they reallocate the funds. A good portion of the funds came from foreign aid. That needs to be questioned on at least two grounds. First, foreign aid as it is managed in this country generally leads to the employment of Canadians. When you take money out of foreign aid, you are taking jobs away from Canadians. We live in a world in which we are the affluent in spite of all our economic problems. There are those who need far more than we do. We make a small contribution to that need through foreign aid, yet we have the unmitigated gall to take money away from foreign aid, to rob money from the Third World in order to appear to create jobs. That is not acceptable. It is not the way we should be going.
Another reallocation item was taking money out of the CHIP Program, an energy program, which would be jobintensive. What jobs are created if you take jobs from a jobintensive Program and put them into a job-creation Program? That does not seem to make a great deal of sense. The New Democratic Party by contrast recommended that we take some of the incentives from the oil industry, which is very highly capitalized and creates few jobs, and redirect those resources to job intensive industries such as housing and forestry. That is
Supply
a way to reallocate money and come up in the balance with more jobs rather than less.
The economic statement of the Minister of Finance has an underlying economic strategy. Not only has he adopted the line of authority, which is to placate the private sector in an attempt to appeal to the business community, but what he has done in real economic terms is that he has given a tax break to those in the very upper income brackets. When the former Minister of Finance brought in his budget in November, he had lower tax rates for those in the upper income brackets, but he closed some of the loopholes. When the present Minister of Finance brought in his statement, he retained the lesser tax rate for the upper income people but reopened the loopholes. Those in the upper income brackets get the tax break while ordinary average Canadians who are struggling to make a living have been given a whopping 40 to 53 per cent tax increase in unemployment insurance premiums.
This is clearly inequitable and does not make any economic sense. I will state why quite clearly. At this moment we have an economy with a high percentage of savings and very weak consumer spending. We have to mobilize those savings and bring them around to stimulate consumer spending in order to get the economy moving and people working. One way to do this would be for those in the highest income brackets, those earning over $40,000 or $50,000, or those 704 people who earn over $100,000 a year and do not pay any tax whatsoever, to pay a fair share, to pay a progressive tax. Those revenues could be used for direct, full-time job creation. That would put money in the pockets of ordinary Canadians. It would get people back to work. Consumer spending would be strengthened, which is what we need to get the economy moving in the direction of recovery.
The economic strategy and the economic statement of the Minister of Finance is wrongheaded. It is out of whack with reality. In effect, it is a drag on the economy.
Unemployment insurance premiums have been increased at a time when most businesses are having a difficult time. For those running a small business, this added tax will make it more difficult to keep employees. Retail trade is down to one-half or one-third of what it was last year. It will be a tough decision to decide whether to keep a sales clerk or put him on the unemployment insurance rolls. The economic strategy in the document does not make any sense in terms of the goal of full employment and the right of Canadians to have a job and a decent income.
I would like to say a little more about the unemployment insurance system. The system is under a great deal of pressure. It was set up to service a lower rate of unemployment. Over the last year, the unemployment insurance caseload has doubled. This has been the experience in the local office in Winnipeg that I visited. The result of this extremely high caseload has resulted in constant delays for the average person applying for unemployment insurance.
One could play the game of trying to find out who is to blame-whether the person returned the card at the right

November 5, 1982
Supply
time, whether the commission sent out the card at the right time, how it got off the computer or how it got in to the computer. Once the process gets off the computer, the delays go on and on. It is a very long and slow process for a person to get unemployment insurance benefits.
I recommend that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) hire an adequate number of people to keep these unemployment insurance claims moving at a decent pace. If he cannot re-program the computer to handle the situation in order to avoid delays, he should hire people to process the claims so that the unemployed do not have to wait for these much needed benefits.
It is not only the average person applying for unemployment insurance benefits who faces these delays but those who are involved with some of the specific job creation programs of which the Government is so proud. There is, for example, the work-sharing program which the Minister is quoted as calling a success. We have learned that it is somewhat less than a success. Many of those who became involved in the worksharing program are now unemployed. The program was supposed to keep them working, yet they are now becoming unemployed. This is because work-sharing was designed as a short-term measure and the economic recession we are now in is long-term.
With regard to unemployment insurance, specifically, I have had complaints from various groups across the country who indicate that after they sign the work-sharing agreement it takes months before they can get their benefits. They have to wait an intolerable length of time. Even after the work sharing has run its course and they are back to being unemployed, there are further delays in order to get back on ordinary unemployment insurance. My colleague will be mentioning problems similar to this with regard to other employment programs, including the Employment Bridging Assistance Program.
I would like to focus now upon the question of those people who have been on unemployment insurance over the last year and are now exhausting their benefits. These are the people who are faced with the prospect of seeking welfare and having to exhaust all of their personal savings. These are the people who are suffering a great deal from the recession in which we are today.
The economic statement of the Minister of Finance indicated that the NEED Program, the job creation program, was going to meet the needs of those who had exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits. The statistics of the Department of Employment indicate some 50,000 to 55,000 people a month are now exhausting their unemployment insurance benefits and the predictions are that this figure will increase to
90.000	per month. The NEED job creation program, even by the Government's own standards, is going to create only some
60.000	jobs. That will cover one month, Mr. Speaker, whereas the NEED Program is supposed to last a period of some 18 months. The economic statement made reference to a previous job creation program of $300 million. That also, by using the
appropriate rule of thumb, would create some 25,000 full-time jobs, which would in no way meet the needs of these people who have exhausted their UIC benefits.
I think it is time for the Government to consider seriously the extension of UIC benefits for another 26 weeks. I say this because, clearly, the Government has failed to meet the need by providing jobs for those people who are exhausting their UIC benefits. In order to be humane and leave people with their self-respect and human dignity, I recommend to the Government that it extend the benefits under the unemployment insurance system.
I say this because the unemployment insurance system was originally set up because the federal Government recognized that it was the prime mover in the national economy and had responsibility for the health of the economy and for employment. It had adopted the goal of full employment, a goal which is essential to Canada and to the roughly two million people today who are unemployed. By extending these benefits, the Government would once again reassert its responsibility in economic matters and show its concern about those people who have no other place to go now but welfare, or exhaust their personal savings.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the second time this week that we have had the opportunity, through an Opposition motion, to discuss the very important question of unemployment in the country, and it happens on a day when we received the latest figures on unemployment. I wish these figures were otherwise than what they are, because they are serious and tragic, but they do create for the Members of this Chamber the requirement to deal with the matter in a straightforward, logical, consistent, and I hope constructive manner.
That is why I was looking forward with some anticipation, Mr. Speaker, to the opening remarks of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) on behalf of the New Democratic Party, which claims, at least in its public utterances, that it is the Party which is concerned about the unemployed. I hope you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, if I express my deep disappointment in what we have heard in the initial contribution in this House, because it was a massive contradiction wrapped up in a ball of misrepresentations, and has added nothing to the kind of debate which we need in this House in order to come to grips with the issues.
I think one of the difficulties we have is that we can very quickly manufacture pseudo events and pseudo truths. It seems the NDP feel that somehow if they say something long enough it will become reality even though it is not based upon fact but concocted somewhere in cuckoo land and makes absolutely no sense at all when it comes to the reality of what we are dealing with. And that is certainly the kind of position we heard from the Hon. Member today.
He began by condemning the NEED Program, saying it is a make-work program, which make no sense, and does not provide jobs that last long. None of this is true, of course,
November 5, 1982

because the Program is designed for 12 months, not 20 weeks. We have said that consistently. It is designed to provide longterm jobs in a productive way. It is having the success of bringing a wide variety of Governments and other institutions together to co-operate in a major effort to deal with the problem of exhaustees. We are trying to put together a program which will provide the alternative to work. None of this was acknowledged by the Hon. Member. Instead, the Hon. Member did nothing but criticize the NEED program, throw scorn upon it and dismiss it, even though it will provide work opportunities for many of those people he talks about.
He takes the position that we must do something about the exhaustees. What did he offer us as a solution? The Hon. Member suggested we should extend unemployment insurance benefits for another 26 weeks. Making a quick calculation, Mr. Speaker, that would probably add something like $3 billion to $4 billion to the cost of the unemployment insurance fund. At the same time, the Hon. Member asked that we not raise unemployment insurance premiums to pay for it because they have already gone up too high. Does he have a secret formula or is there a tree out there, wherever the NDP make their policy, that they can shake to get money? Do they not realize that unemployment insurance is paid by the employees, the employers and the taxpayers? If you provide for an extension of benefits for 26 weeks at an additional cost of approximately $3 billion, somebody has to pay for it.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, to add one contradiction upon another, we also have the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) saying the deficit should not be raised any higher, that the deficit should stay where it is. So we are faced with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James saying we should put another $3 billion into the fund, but do not raise the premiums, do not raise the deficit.
So where is the money going to come from? The conventional knee-jerk answer of the NDP is "tax the rich". Yet we see in today's paper that profits are down in most major companies in this country by 44 per cent. We have other members of the NDP saying we should put more money into investment and research and development. But where does the money come from? It comes form the profits of the companies which the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James wants to tax further. When you add that all up, Mr. Speaker, it simply does not make sense. You cannot add more benefits, cut back taxes, not raise premiums, or put more money into investment, without getting the money from somewhere. The money has to come from taxpayers or by running up a deficit. It has to come from some source. It does not appear magically on a doorstep because the tooth fairy put it there. Yet that seems to be the source of inspiration for the economic policy of the NDP. They are not offering us anything that is consistent, logical or rational. They are simply trying to package together a whole round of mythologies and misrepresentations in the hope of gaining support. So, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to puncture holes in that particular bit of fantasy spun out by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James.

I feel badly because we had to raise premiums, but we have to make a choice. We have to say to the unemployed workers that if they want to continue to receive their benefits, then that cost must be shared by the broader base of workers and employers across Canada. That is a good philosophy which has stood us in good stead in times of crisis, times of recession. People are prepared to share. Those who have employment are prepared to offer some of their stipend to help those unemployed.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, contrary to the position taken by the Hon. Member who obviously has not done his homework, the premium level was established after very extensive discussion and consultation with labour unions and employers. We asked them what their point of view was. I know the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) does not know what consultation is. He does not believe in it because he does not practise it. But we do, and we went out over the summer and fall and discussed with a wide variety-
Don't give us that line.

It seems, Mr. Speaker, that we have pushed the Hon. Member's panic button again and all we are hearing is a loud wail.
The fact of the matter is that we did consult with employers and unions as to the appropriate level for the premiums. They all admitted that premiums would have to rise, and they said properly so in order that we can share the burden. They asked us not to take them up to the full rate required to exhaust the benefits, and we did not do that. We are contributing $1 billion to the unemployment insurance fund through Government financing in order to carry the burden for the unemployed through that system. But is the New Democratic Party prepared to recognize that? Are they prepared to recognize the best advice we got from the private sector and the unions? Oh no, they have their own little conjuring machine which sort of spins out these wild fantasies about how we are going to do all the different things we should do and somehow there will be the dollars necessary to pay for it. It just does not work that way, Mr. Speaker. That is not the way the system works. You have to have a balance sheet, and unfortunately they will never have to meet that balance sheet because they will never be in Government.
Let us spend a moment, Mr. Speaker, talking about the other parts of the unemployment insurance system because other Members of that caucus opposite have been rising to their feet in great condemnation of the unemployment insurance system. They do not seem to recognize that across the country in many cases the number of applications has almost doubled. I can give some figures which might be of interest to Hon. Members of the House. If you look at the figures for September, 1981 and September, 1982, the number of claims we received went from 1.8 milion to 2.7 million. In certain regions of the country, particularly in British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec, the claim load has gone up over 100 per cent.

Because of that we have put in place a number of corrective measures. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James said: "Why not add new people?" I would like to inform him that he is a little late with his advice, because three months ago we appropriated an additional 1,200 person-years, we have finished training these people and they are going into the offices right now to work on the additional unemployment claim load. You would think he might have spent a little time learning those facts. Instead, he simply condemns the hundreds of employees in the UIC who have been spending countless hours of overtime, working six or seven days a week, to try and meet the problems of people as well as the claim load. But oh no, they have no concern or sympathy for those working people who are going above and beyond the call of duty to try and meet the crisis. They simply criticize and condemn those workers.
That is not true.

The fact of the matter is that we have put in a number of measures. In addition to the 1200 person-years, we have established separate adjudication centres to deal with the problem. We have relaxed certain criteria as far as the Auditor General will allow us to. We have worked with business and labour to try and get a better reporting system. We have established special regional task forces so that members of the Commission can move from one area where the demand is low to where it is high. We have been using those measures through the summer and fall and have reduced the backlog as a result.
We have not solved the problem, Mr. Speaker, I admit that. But we are working on it and we have a lot of very fine people in the Commission who are devoting their time to making it work.
Hear, hear!
Agreed.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we get this kind of resolution which absolutely condemns the Commission and the people who work for it.
Don't pass the buck.

That is the NDP for you. That is the Party which likes to say it is full of generosity and tolerance for the working people. They sure do not care about the people in our Commission who are working overtime, double time, to get the product out. They are making very major sacrifices to make sure that the system delivers.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is saying: "Well, part of the problem is the additional employment programs you have brought in. They are putting too much pressure on the system." After all, there are some snags in the system.
They are not working.

The fact of the matter is that when you have
180,000	workers enrolled in a work sharing program, a program which has averted 75,000 lay-offs, it seems to me that is an initiative which should be applauded, not condemned, by
the Hon. Member for Winnipeg, St.-James. We have saved the jobs of 75,000 workers in the country through that one program alone. Again, you would think the NDP might have some concern about that. They might take some interest in that program and help us to improve it. If there are problems, then we will respond to them and put the people to work. I invite Members of the NDP caucus, when they have a problem, to bring it to my attention and I will try to correct it. But let them not put up in this House this kind of resolution and make a blanket condemnation of initiatives which are providing basic security and job protection for over 180,000 workers in this country. I will not accept that kind of condemnation because, as we all know, it is based on a know nothing attitude, not on a realistic appraisal of how to correct the problem and come to grips with the issues we face.
1 think, Mr. Speaker, this resolution does nothing for the honour, standing or stature of the NDP in this House. It is not constructive or positive, it offers no solutions; it is simply caustic and negative in its tone. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James continued that particular negative panegyric when he got to his feet to punch holes in the efforts we are making to help people bridge this very serious recession we are in. Those Programs, Mr. Speaker, are working. Not only the NEED Program, but the Training Program of $1 billion.
I was fascinated by the Leader of the NDP who again was only about a year late coming up with a proposal. He said "I have a brand new solution for the problems of the economy; let us have a new training program". Where has he been for the last year when this House passed the National Training Act? Where was be when this House appropriated $1 billion for new training across this country? Have they been asleep so long? Are they so far out of touch that they do not even know what is going on in this Parliament, in this House, and then they propose something already done as part of their great solution to the Canadian crisis?. 1 think Canadians expect far more from the Opposition critics at this point in time. They expect far more than borrowing ideas and concocting fantasy. They expect the Opposition to be working with the Programs we have initiated in order to help make them work.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we have the NEED Program, a $500 million program which can be added to with the co-operation of the Provinces and the private sector and which will provide over 60,000 jos. Not the short-term jobs the Hon. Member pretends it will provide, but jobs which will last up to a year; jobs which will build fishing wharves in Newfoundland and water systems in Nova Scotia; jobs in the forest industry in British Columbia and in the cities of Canada developing municipal services and renovating housing. That is the kind of work this Program is intended to do, and if we can get the cooperation of Members of this House as we are now getting it from the Provinces and the private sector of this country, we will have a Program which will provide major support and real
November 5, 1982

hope for the unemployed in this country at a time when they need that support and hope the most.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, seldom has a Royal Commission been announced and established with such a lack of conviction!
I want to make some remarks in this debate on the motion of the New Democratic Party, primarily with respect to the programs of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). However, in light of the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last night and in question period today, perhaps I ought to offer some remarks with respect to the proposed Royal Commission first of all.
1 have no difficulty in accepting the principle of a Royal Commission. Royal Commissions have been established in this country for over a century and on three or four occasions have dealt with employment matters and economic prospects. They are usually two or three years in the making and take about a year and a half for consideration of the subject. That is generally enough time for most of the recommendations not to be accepted.
When the Prime Minister spoke about a Royal Commission earlier today he mentioned the Rowell-Sirois Royal Commission which was established in 1937 and reported about 1940. It was hardly ever heard from again, except in the lecture halls of universities.
We do not have great difficulty with the idea of a Royal Commission but rather with the way it is being approached. We would like to have a Royal Commission. Indeed, in the past we have urged that one be appointed, but we have two difficulties with the way it is being done here. First, it is being presented as a smokescreen behind which the Government can hide the unemployment figures as the number of people unemployed in this country grows. Second, we have the feeling that it is more related to the Prime Minister's leadership difficulties at the convention this weekend than it has to do with any serious and sincere concern for the economic problems that affect the people of this country. We recognize that the appointment of Mr. Macdonald is absolutely necessary for the weekend, but I do not think this is the kind of approach to

November 5, 1982
Supply
Canada's economic problems that will enhance any trust, if there is any left, in this Government.
If there is to be a Royal Commission, we have a couple of ideas for the Government to consider when it actually sets up this Commission. The Commission should deal with both longterm and short-term problems. It should deal with specific facts and figures in relation to the analysis of what has happened to us in the past ten years. It should make recommendations for the immediate future as well as for the long term in terms of technological change between now and the turn of the century.
I think the Commission should also deal with those aspects of Government policy which have caused such incredible difficulty for this country. I refer to policies with respect to interest rates and the National Energy Program-at least, those aspects of it that have destroyed investor confidence. The Commission should deal with research and development and with the establishment of national training centres across the country so that people can be trained for jobs in the future. This Commission should not be one of those that is drawn out for two and three years. We hope that a deadline will be established of something in the order of six months.

speechtext:
That is right. I fear that the idea of this Commission will not even last beyond the weekend or until the Liberals have dealt with their convention. It is really a shoddy trick.
A Royal Commission should be independent. It should not be a vehicle for the Liberal Party to politicize its problems with respect to its responsibilities to the Canadian people. I suggest that this Commission be made up of three people, one of whom should represent labour in the interests of the working people. The second member of this Commission should be a woman, because there are so many more women now adversely affected than before with respect to employment opportunities. This three-person independent Commission should be dealing with both short-range and long-range problems. That is desirable so long as it is impartial and independent. The difficulty with such a Royal Commission is that it is simply playing politics on the part of the Liberal Party and its setting up has not been motivated by any sincere concern to do something for the people of Canada facing current economic difficulties.
I now want to deal with some of the matters raised by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Every time people make suggestions either inside or outside of this House these days, the Minister of Employment and Immigration keeps saying "Let's co-operate; why keep attacking me?" He gets very concerned that somehow we do not believe what he has to say.
The only specific proposal that this House has seen dealing with unemployment since the House opened a week ago has been the proposal made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to establish a Program called NEED. This Program is to create 60,000 short-term jobs to begin in January, at a
cost of about half a billion dollars. Make no mistake about the purpose of that Program. It is not to create jobs but to create an opportunity to allow those whose unemployment insurance benefits are exhausted and would then go on to welfare to requalify for UIC. To that extent, the Program is worthwhile. There is not a Member in this House who is opposed to opportunities for employment so that people can requalify for unemployment insurance. But anybody who suggests in all honesty that this is a job creation Program that deals with 1.75 million unemployed by creating 60,000 short-term jobs, I will not go so far as to say is dishonest, but is certainly in total ignorance of what is happening on the streets of this country. People are hurting yet the Government fools around with that kind of Program and this nonsense about a Royal Commission.
The priority of the Government should be to provide longterm jobs for people. The unemployment rate among the young of this country, those between the ages of 15 and 24, is 21 per cent. These people will not be affected by the Program which the Minister offers. They are not on unemployment insurance because these are the ones applying for their first jobs. Our graduates from colleges and universities have an unemployment rate this year, according to the figures this morning, of close to 19 per cent. The Government has not even bothered to address their problems.
When the Minister seeks co-operation and wonders why we attack his policies, he has forgotten that when he took over the Ministry two years ago the unemployment rate was 7.4 per cent. The number of unemployed at that time was 854,000 people. The rate two years later is 12.7 per cent and there are
1,521,000	people officially unemployed in this country. This Minister has presided over the largest decline of employment in this country since the great depression. I can understand why he gets thin-skinned about people who, on behalf of their own constituents, are attacking his lack of action. He knows his record as Minister has been the worst since the depression.
When a person is responsible for the doubling of unemployment and the loss of 750,000 jobs, I suppose putting up a smokescreen is about the only thing he can do. It is a smokescreen of numbers. The Minister of Finance's Program costing about half a billion dollars and creating 60,000 jobs was not even planned. When that Program was announced the Government was not even aware what budget it would have. It talked airily about participation by the other Provinces to bring in $1.2 billion. The federal Government would put in $500 million, with additions from the Provinces. It is now clear from the Minister's flying around, because we have now had a public statement from the Provinces that he will not have anywhere close to that amount of money for his budget. He not only has no budget but he has no program.
Did anyone hear one program which the Minister was suggesting that was new? There was not one idea. There was not one new program. The Minister was not only looking for ideas from the Provinces or anybody else because he did not have any ideas of his own, but he just had a budget that was
November 5, 1982

brought in for the occasion. Rumours tell us that the Minister got permission from the Cabinet to do this about 24 hours before the Minister of Finance made his speech. The program bears the marks of having given no thought to the actual onstreet delivery of jobs.
The Minister's problem is that he has been unable to approach the House in a kind of honest fashion that says "Here are the problems. Here are the difficulties we see with certain solutions. Here is what we would like to do in the short run and here is what we would like to do in the long run." That is the way in which most people would approach their responsibilities. He does not do that. The Minister of Employment and Immigration just announces figures, reannounces them, scrambles them, multiplies them, permutates them and combines them.
People across the country are at a loss to understand what those figures mean, but what we do know for sure after two years is that every time the Minister announces a new program, unemployment goes up. For people on the streets that is reality. Unemployment simply gets worse as we hear more and more figures announced and reannounced.
The Minister finished his speech in relation to what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) said today by saying that this Program will have people back to work in the mines, in the fishing industry, in the manufacturing sector in Ontario, and that we will have people back to work in British Columbia. That is what the Minister does every time. The difficulty is that people know the reality. People live the reality. Increasingly, the federal Government is being brought into disrepute by that kind of publicity seeking, with no reality in terms of actual jobs delivered.
If there is any doubt in anyone's mind that the program announced by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration is only to do with so-called exhaustees, I suggest they read the report that was issued. It said that the program is specifically designed to benefit those who exhaust unemployment insurance benefits and would otherwise fall back on welfare. We agree with that. That is what must be done, but there are two problems involved. One, the figures which are used by the Minister which set out
60,000	jobs-even if it is that many-are about 25,000 too short. The statistics the Government is using with respect to unemployment are far lower than the actual unemployment. Mark my words, Mr. Speaker, it will discover that it will have to return to the House or make an announcement that it will need to increase that fund, because the program offered will not cover all those people who are on unemployment and will fall on welfare.
The statistics this morning indicate that this is already happening, let alone what will happen next month and the following months. While there is a short-term problem, the Government's short-term program will not even cover those who are currently drawing unemployment insurance and about to fall into welfare.

Second, it is an absolutely cruel hoax by the Government to suggest that this type of program has anything to do with those who are not on unemployment insurance and going on to welfare. It does not affect the million other people who are simply unemployed. For that reason the Minister is in difficulty when he makes those statements because he promises far too much. People depend on his announcements because they accept what he says as a Minister of the Crown to be the truth. As someone said this morning about a provincial Minister whom he had already seen, "He came here looking for publicity, money and ideas. He got none of them."
There is an interesting column in this morning's Citizen which I believe makes the case. The title is: "Job Creation Plan Still a Mystery". Indeed it is, Mr. Speaker. It is still a mystery. The Minister flies, he announces, multiplies and combines, but no jobs of any significance are created for anyone.
Part of the NDP motion also deals with the way in which the unemployment insurance system works. I believe that the Minister made a good defence of the quality of those working in his Department, who try very hard to fill the orders. When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James indicated that there were thousands of problems with the way unemployment insurance is administered, he was right. I suggest that it was unfair for the Minister to simply say we should not accuse the workers in that Department of not working hard. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James was not suggesting that. He is trying to impress upon the Minister that there are thousands of problems with how the Unemployment Insurance Program is administered.
The fact of the matter is that every Member in the House can produce a file such as I have-which is only last week's alone-of people who have legitimate concerns over the administration of unemployment insurance. I expect that the Minister would listen to those concerns and act upon them rather than simply attack someone who legitimately questions the administration of the program.
Let me select one letter from about 30 which I received last week. This is an appropriate letter because it points out the problems of UIC. This letter was written to "Change Canada". This person wrote:
I watched your Television promotion on training Canadians for trades of the future. One thing that I am confused about is the fact that I am one of those Canadians given the chance to be retrained at Humber College (Canada Manpower Retraining) for which I had used all of my Unemployment Insurance Benefits only to find that after long hours of homework and sacrifice I am now in the position of having no employment.
I have inquired for employment at over 140 companies dealing in this field. Being without employment I have taken a job at a temporary placement service which can be of no benefit to me and my career change.
Now I find, that after graduating on December 4, 1981, no one is in the position to hire me due to economic conditions. 1 cannot even get a junior position in my field! (Numerical Control Machine Program) and no one will give me a position in labour because they feel I will leave when 1 find an opportunity to enter my field.
So could you please answer this question? Is this new program you are offering designed to give false hopes in the future or is it sincere considering the Employment Departments are going to import 20,000 skilled workers? Where does this leave Canadians like myself?

All the letters that most Members receive either deal with the administration and the problem of getting service in terms of UI payouts or, even more importantly in the long run, with trying to get employment in the types of jobs that the Government, over the last number of years, has seen fit to train people for.
The all-Party committee in its estimation of the track record of the Government in producing training for jobs that are available, which is called "Work for Tomorrow", utterly condemned the Government's handling of Manpower programs primarily because they lead to dead-end jobs, if any job at all. This was the view of all parties in that committee.
This has been the problem throughout when trying ot deal with the Minister and the Government generally in terms of understanding what is actually happening to ordinary Canadians in towns, villages and cities all across Canada as they try to cope with the deepening recession. Canadians, and indeed our Party, do not want to blame the Government; it is just so difficult to convey to it that when it only gives us numbers and multiplies them and publicizes those figures, it creates that lack of trust and credibility which is so entrenched in the minds of Canadians that even when it brings out a program that may be helpful, people have difficulty believing it.
This afternoon a number of Members from the New Democratic Party will be making points and offering suggestions in support of their motion. We will support that motion because the Minister and his Government seem far more concerned either with its publicity or its internal politics than with seriously dealing with the recession which is deepening every day.
The unemployment figures which were released this morning are the highest since the depression. There is 12.7 per cent of the Canadian work force unemployed and 21 per cent of those are between the ages of 15 and 24. Those are the young Canadians who are just starting out in their work life. As well, many towns and villages are economically decimated by the deepening recession while the Government does so little to help those towns and villages which we in the House know so well are so adversely affected that they are unable to deal with their own economic base. Hamilton, for example, has unemployment at 15 per cent.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I will conclude by saying that unless the Government begins to take the unemployment difficulties in this country seriously, it will reap social problems in this country which will take decades to rectify. It is time for the Government to stop worrying about publicity and politics and to start working hard to ensure that long-term, useful programs are developed for the people out on the street who are crying out for them.
