speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was with some dismay and deep regret, I must say, that I heard anything but positive remarks from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) earlier this morning. There is an old saying with which I think we are all
familiar. It is: "If at first you don't succeed, try and try again."
The Minister's feelings were obviously hurt. He said that we do not congratulate him when he tries. He does try, Mr. Speaker. He tries and tries and tries again. However, the first part of that equation is: "If at first you don't succeed-" I, and I think all Canadians, are only left with the very clear impression that the Minister has failed again and again and again and that is why he must keep on trying. That is a sorry situation.
There is such an absolute myriad of mismanagement, disorganization and unco-ordination in the conduct of one employment program after another that no one could believe it is only the fault of some hard working public employees. The Minister himself said that those employees have been working overtime for hours every day, coming in with fresh recruits, having to train at least hundreds to do a job for which the Department is so ill prepared. No one will blame those people. I thought it was a very cheap shot by the Minister to suggest that we were going after the hard working employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. No such thought was in our minds. In fact, I would pay a compliment. There have been fuddle-ups in the EBAP Program, within the Salmon Enhancement Program in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia and others. We have actually seen pictures on television of unemployed Canadians who were left with no cash at all because of the fumbling of the Minister, his Government and Department. One of them was lent money out of the pockets of an employee of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. With the restraints imposed upon those hard working employees by the Government, they can ill afford to pass out that money, especially to people who, if we go by the track record of UIC delays, really do not know when or whether their next benefit cheques will come. So it was a cheap shot by the Minister. The Minister has failed and failed again, not the employees of the UIC and not the hard working employees elsewhere in his Department.
Before 1 list the catalogue of horror stories, both specific and more general, I want to make a comment on a peculiar announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of the establishment of yet another Royal Commission into Canada's economic prospects. It is fascinating to some of us who recall history to find that we should once again have a Prime Minister and Government Members who continually pile parliamentary committees upon Royal Commissions. That was the description in the well known poem of Frank Scott entitled "W.L.M.K." In reference to our late Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, he wrote:
The height of his ambition
Was to pile a Parliamentary Committee on a
Royal Commission
My, my, things have not changed very much, have they? They have not changed at all. I wonder whether this is the
November 5, 1982

resurrection of Walter Gordon, who headed a Royal Commission on Canada's economic prospects approximately 20 years ago. Will this one turn out to be such a failure? Will the person appointed to run it be the same kind of failure, according to that Government opposite as well as many Canadians, as was the author of that report? When will we receive a regurgitated Herb Gray report on foreign investment in Canada? Is that the next one? When will we get a regurgitated form of a Carter Royal Commission on Taxation? Will we get that, too? Will we have one regurgitated rehash and resurrection after another?
If that is all the Government has to offer, it ought to get out now because there is no sense in us being positive with its Members. All they want to do is hide behind one more commission, behind the hard working Public Service, to screen them from the attacks so legitimately deserved by the Government. What a sorry mess. What a sorry prospect for Canadians who, like many of my constituents who I visited this summer, are almost without hope because of the Government's constant inaction and delays.
I think the most heartrending experience I have ever had was in visiting the homes of some of my former workmates at B.C. Timber's Kootenay forest products sawmill in Nelson which has been shut down for almost a year. The first group was dropped from the seniority list, after being laid off for 18 months just a few days ago. I am not stereotyping here, but I think that almost all Hon. Members in this House and most Canadians would agree that, in spite of their Catholicism,Ital-ian-Canadians are almost the very picture of the Protestant work ethic. No group is recognized as working harder and longer and using credit less until the advent of the larcenous interest policies of the last few years, both the Conservative and Liberal interest rate policies. Hardly any member of that community even went into debt to buy a house. To start with, they would buy a small house. They would build and improve. They would pool their labour together with their neighbours and families.
Now we see that after decades of hard and honest work, many of these people own not only their own homes, but also second homes and third homes. However, because the only industrial operations in their community have been shut down for either a year or a year and a half, they do not have any tenants left because anyone who does not have deep roots has moved away. These home owners are in a state of crisis. Some of the hardest cases that I know of, and I use that term in a complimentary way, involve guys who would give me the roughest time at any union meeting we ever attended. I have been seated at their kitchen tables when these men have openly cried in front of me and admitted to me that on alternate days-because they are still pretty strong-they think that perhaps the sawmill will open again, that they may survive and will be in a position to send their children to ice-skating classes again. They think that maybe they will be able to afford to put decent food on the table on a regular basis again and purchase a few building materials to make improvements to their houses so they can take advantage of some of the other Government programs. But then there are the other days when they look at the sorry morass around them across this country, the morass
Supply
that this Government sits on top of, and they wonder if they will ever get out of that hole.
I have seen them break down and cry, and these are pretty tough people, these hard working guys, some of the toughest I have ever had the honour of working beside. When they work they work hard, and when they build they build well. They want a chance to build, a chance to contribute, because it hurts anyone's pride to be left out of the productive sector of our society. It is exactly these people and their neighbors who have never had to resort to going on UIC benefits before, and it tears their guts out to think they may have to go on welfare. I will not continue to talk about how these people, no matter how hard pressed they are, feel. It is a sad story and having once stated it, I do not believe we need to go over it again and again.
However, I do want to refer to some specific problems. In my own home town of Nelson and in the surrounding community, there are a number of programs under the Employment Bridging Assistance Program. However, one of the problems is that if one is approved and hired under such a Program, one is taken off the regular UIC computers and is entered on to a manual system of benefits payment. Quoting from a newspaper article in my own local paper, "If you work, you wait longer for your cheque than you would if you do not work". That is the dilemma being faced by unemployed Nelson area workers who have opted for make-work projects funded under the federal-provincial Employment Bridging Assistance Program. That is exactly what has happened because of the fumbling within the Minister's area of responsibility. If one goes to work for one's benefits, one does not receive any money for weeks. When I say weeks, I do not mean two or three. One can be cut off regular benefits which one has received for a long time and then can wait two to 12 weeks before one begins to receive any money out of the benefits one has paid for. That is inexcusable and intolerable and these delays have been going on for months.
Do Hon. Members want to know what happened to one of these UIC employees who led a group of his fellow EBAP employees down to the welfare office so they would have social assistance to provide food on their tables? He had the audacity, I suppose, according to the Government's views, to complain on CBC Radio about the maladministration of the Program, not only because of delays in payments, but also because administration costs going to the employers of record had risen from $50 a week to $100 to $200 per week per man. He was fired from the UIC Program the next day and his employer of record said that it had nothing to do with his work.
Those of us who know the history of Canada, especially that of working people, realize that not so long ago it was not uncommon for employees of Government and employees in private industry to be fired for exercising their God-given right to freedom of speech. But have we now reached the point

November 5, 1982
Supply
where one can be fired from the unemployment rolls for it? How ridiculous can they get? I raised this matter the other day in the House. When that employee sought redress through his former union representative-of course he does not pay dues any more but he has a retirement card-he looked at the laws of the land and found out that his provincial Government, the partner in this mess with the federal Government had wiped out the Employment Standards Act of British Columbia as it applied to people who work under the Employment Bridging Assistance Program. I expect that has happened in other Provinces as well.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) is present but the Minister of Employment and Immigration is not. I ask him whether the Government will assume some responsibility for the conditions and terms of work of people employed under a program which is essentially its program. If the Provinces, either by collusion with the federal Government or acting independently-British Columbia does some funny things some times-do not look after the basic and fundamental rights of employees, surely we must ask the federal Government and the Minister of Labour to confirm that this is a matter of federal jurisdiction. Then a case could be made and the basic rights, imperfect as they are outlined in our federal labour laws, will apply to these EBAP employees.
I should like to turn to a slightly less serious note but one that is very important. The Minister of Employment and Immigration wanted some cases. What about an unemployed construction worker in Vancouver who was denied his claim for benefits because he was pregnant? Perhaps this example is on the humorous side, but I would like to quote his language, it is not mine. He went down to the unemployment insurance office and said, "I know I am getting screwed but I ain't pregnant". The information I have is that he is still waiting, and he has been waiting weeks and weeks. Anyone can slip up.
I am not suggesting that this sort of extreme example, which gives the worst impression, often goes on. There are more odd stories than we would like to ever admit or think about.
I would like to refer to another case of an unemployed logger who has waited 12 weeks for his benefits. For some weeks he has, along with other claimants, been launching a class action law suit, assisted by his union, the International Woodworkers, against the Minister and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Why is it that people have to shell out their own money, whether it is money that they have put into union dues or out of their own pockets, to get some attention paid to foul-ups and unconscionable delays in payments of regular UIC benefits to which they are entitled and for which they have paid many times over? These are not lazy people. Many of them have not been on UIC before. They have paid into it, they want to work, and they have a right to expect their benefits. It is not enough to say that, "we are working all our employees overtime, hiring more people and training more people." My God, could they not see it coming?

Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper), the mover of this motion, earlier today, the Minister of Finance said that this is a time when the value of people's homes is going down and when prices on a wide range of commodities were falling. I am not trying to be an alarmist, but the other day the Minister of Finance said that we were in a state of depression. Those were his words, not mine. That is exactly the situation we are in.
Also a few moments ago the Minister of Employment made reference to consultation and that somehow my NDP colleagues and I do not want good consultation with anyone.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate because the subject matter is of great concern to me and the constitutents I represent. It is fitting for me to congratulate the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) as well as the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) who earlier in the week had this very same subject matter placed before the House of Commons. I like to see issues of great importance not only to my constituency but to the national economy placed before the Parliament of Canada.
In reading through the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James, I note that the tone of that motion is a harsh one. I agree with some parts of the motion. The Hon. Member attacks the system of unemployment insurance and attacks a system whereby there are numerous delays, claims and appeals. Members of Parliament have files of people who are encountering these difficulties. It is fair to place before the Parliament of Canada, the Minister and his officials as well as Government members those specific instances so that they can be examined.
It is awfully unfair for the Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party to talk only of the problems and not the solutions. Anyone can list the number of people unemployed in his or her community. Anyone, particularly on the Opposition benches, can list the number of businesses that have gone into bankruptcy or receivership as a result of the world economic recession. Unfortunately, when mentioning the problem they forget some very pertinent elements, such as the world recession of which Canada is a part. They fail to mention that there are 30 million people unemployed in the OECD countries. If Canadians for one moment think or hope that somehow that world recession is going to pass us by and leave us alone, they are sadly mistaken.
Supply
When listening to the Opposition, particularly the New Democratic Party, one would think there is only one Government in this country. Yes, there is a national Government, but there are also provincial and municipal Governments and they have to play their part.
Not only the public sector but the private sector has a role to play in terms of changing and turning our economy around to provide the jobs we all want. I find it somewhat repugnant to have the Hon. Member for Rosedale, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James or the New Democratic Party try to have this corner of sympathy for the working man to themselves. All Members of Parliament regardless of their political ideology share that concern and want to do something about unemployment.
The Government has introduced the six and five program on wages and prices. It has to be accepted that a 6 per cent world or 6 per cent inflation rate is a lot better than the 12 or 14 per cent world we have had for the last number of months and will provide businesses with confidence and the incentive to reinvest. It is essential that that program work.
I find Members of Parliament, particularly those opposite, questioning the substance of that program, sneering at it as opposed to getting together with a collective will as a national parliament to support that program. It is in the best interest of every working man and woman in this country to have inflation reduced substantially and to have prices reduced as much possible in order to have our economy turn around.
There are certain facts that even the Opposition, although they talk about the problems, have forgotten to mention. I talked about provincial Governments. We ought not to forget our responsibilities as a national Government, but provincial Governments have a role to play as well. What has the provincial Government of my Province of Nova Scotia done? They are of a different political stripe than we. They have had taxes upon taxes, particularly on industries in my constituency. It is very difficult.
The Government of Canada has introduced a Program funded to the tune of $500 million called the NEED Program. I am somewhat concerned that the New Democratic Party would make jokes and laugh about such a Program. The Program not only requires money from other levels of Government, but requires a sense of co-operation by municipal and provincial Governments to make it work.
It is not the time for us in Canada, regardless of our political ideology, to play that game. The problem is too serious. We need to have jobs in this country and we need them now. To those individuals opposite who want to engage in political rhetoric and political gamesmanship, I say I do not want any part of it. As a member of the national Government, 1 want to co-operate with my provincial and municipal Governments to see that people get back to work, and do so right away.
The Hon. Member who spoke prior to me made some remarks about the Minister of Employment and Immigration

November 5, 1982
Supply
(Mr. Axworthy) not being in the House today. That is correct, he is away. He is attending a national convention at the present time. He is discussing issues and resolutions pertaining to jobs, job creation and the economic development of this country. That is important. The Hon. Member has on this occasion and indeed on many other occasions taken upon himself to resort to low and undignified tactics in this House.
The Department of Employment and Immigration is not the only arm of the Government of Canada. There are numerous other Departments that are actively involved in an attempt to create jobs in Canada and to create them right away.
I mention to the Hon. Member that in my own riding in the last number of weeks and months the Department of Fisheries has made moneys available for the creation of numerous jobs. I refer to the very small communities of South Bar, Lingan, Barrachois Cove, False Bay Beach and Little Harbour in Richmond County. Thousands of dollars have been poured into those small communities. They are not Vancouver, Toronto or Montreal but small communities. The Government has put this money into those communities to build facilities to assist the fisherman who, too, is a working person. This is very important, but we do not hear anything positive coming from those on that side. They never want to highlight the moneys which the Government of Canada spends in their areas. As I said at the outset, their sole purpose is to emphasize the problem and not talk about the solution. Part of the solution is making certain that the federal Government and its agencies expedite the moneys they have budgeted under this capital program to get jobs moving in this country.
I have had consultations with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc). I have emphasized that it is absolutely essential for him and his Department to expedite each and every proposal that is budgeted for in his Department so that jobs, construction and a variety of economic spin-offs will result from those initiatives. Housing, Mr. Speaker, is vital. As the House knows, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) put additional sums of money into those programs. That also is part of the solution. It is not the entire solution and I would be less than honest if I tried to suggest in this Chamber, the highest court in this country, that we have all the solutions and answers. As a national Government, we have to accept our responsibilities and put into place the best programs based on the amounts of money available. Even the New Democratic Party has broken away from its longstanding tradition of not increasing the federal deficit any longer.
1 am somewhat saddened, however, by the NDP and the Conservative Party of Canada because there is a sense of hypocrisy when they talk about job creation and job security. In my own riding we are fighting tooth and nail to save two heavy water plants. The NDP laughed because at their national conference they said they were not in favour of the nuclear industry. They said in the House of Commons that the two heavy water plants should be closed. The Progressive Conservative Party said basically the same thing, in what the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee said, in what the former minister of Finance said when he intimated in his
questions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) that they ought to be closed. Yet Hon. Members opposite have the gall to come before this Chamber and say they are concerned, they want to have job creation, have jobs maintained and have security. I find a great deal of hypocrisy coming from the other side of the House, which concerns me greatly. I sat in this Chamber when the Hon. Member for Rosedale brought in his motion earlier this week. I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James. I tried to get one hint of some positive notion they might have in terms of job creation or of stimulating the Canadian economy, and absolutely nothing was forthcoming. It is intellectually dishonest to say, on the one hand, yes, I am concerned about the unemployed and, on the other hand, not to propose anything of assistance. I think that is shameful on the part of the Opposition in this Chamber.
The Conservative Party throughout this country has a responsibility. Every municipal government has a responsibility. We, the Government of Canada, also have a responsibility, and that is to put those programs into place so that we can assist in some real way in alleviating the unemployment problem in this country. The Minister has articulated today the number of programs which are in place and the additional moneys which will be forthcoming for those programs. It is not the panacea for all the ills of the unemployed. I think it would be dishonest on my part if I even suggested that. But it is equally dishonest for the Opposition Parties to stand in their place when there is a national concern like the unemployment issue and merely talk of the problem but provide no solution.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, the Parties opposite are not doing their job. I think it is high time we put political rhetoric aside and collectively supported the Government's policy of six and five, that we supported the principles of fairness and sharing so that those that have, will share with those who do not. That is key, Mr. Speaker, in terms of changing around the Canadian economy. I suggest today, as I have in previous discussions with various Ministers, that the national Government has to continue to examine, through debate and various discussions, the programs we have put into place. We have to expedite some of our capital projects as quickly as possible. We have to do this with a demonstrated spirit of co-operation with other levels of Government and, indeed, the private sector. When inflation prices come down and interest rates come down, I think the road to recovery is not far off, but we must work together as Members of Parliament, not just solely as members of a constituency. The problems are too serious to be shoved aside.
In concluding my remarks, I want to go on record now, as a Member who represents a constituency which has high unemployment, as expressing appreciation to the Minister, to his Parliamentary Secretary and, indeed, to all the members of the Public Service of that Department, for the sensitivity and cooperation they have bestowed on my constituency which is encountering some grave times. I assure you, Mr. Speaker,
November 5, 1982

that the individuals in my constituency, who are hard pressed by unemployment, are aware of those who proposed the quick fix. It is just like the old medicine man when he came around with a bottle of medicine and tried to perpetrate a fraud on the people. The people knew this was not going to be a cure for the illness. I suggest to the Opposition, therefore, let us be honest, put the facts on the table and come to grips with our problems in a co-operative way. Let us have programs for Canadians and forget the political rhetoric which the Party opposite is so good at spreading in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is, as usual, a pleasure to follow the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall). The Hon. Member and I have profoundly different views as to what is wrong in Canada and what needs to be done to make it right. The Parliamentary Secretary asks for solutions. He asks the Members of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada for solutions. Well, Mr. Speaker, you cannot have a solution without first understanding the problem. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has admitted we are in a recession. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his public television broadcast would have you believe that that recession is a consequence of the world-wide economic situation. You would have to be blind not to realize, that, of course, there is a world-wide problem. But other industrialized nations are not in recession. That is a unique Canadian condition caused by Canadians, and if the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy would like a solution to the current problem, can I make one very simple suggestion? There are 147 members of his Party elected to this House. There is a distance of 20 feet to be crossed over to this side of the House to cause a general federal election to be held in this country so that individual Canadians can have a choice as to the future economic direction of this country. That, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Hon. Members of this House, is the only solution that will work, because this is a recession brought on primarily, by fear of the federal Government of Canada and what it will do to individuals. It is a fear brought on by the track record of the present Government. It is fear brought to the hearts of Canadians by what the Members opposite have done to this country. It is fear brought to the hearts of Canadians by what the Members opposite have done to this country. It is fear brought on by both previous and current legislation. It is a well known fact, Mr. Speaker, that in the two years since the Liberal Government came back into office some $18 billion-$18 billion-of capita) has left this country to be invested in homes, condominiums and factories in the U.S., and in oil wells and drilling platforms around the world. This money was chased out of this country-unwillingly, but chased-by federal Government policies, and with every dollar of that money there went jobs.
The fear has grown in Canadians, Mr. Speaker. Two days ago, on Tuesday of this week, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) introduced into the Senate of Canada a Bill which is a direct attack on property rights. There is a Bill before this Chamber, dealing with Public Works, which is a direct attack on the right of Canadians to
Supply
own property. These are two current pieces of legislation, and they go together, Mr. Speaker, with the National Energy Program which took 25 per cent of property held by Canadians in the oil industry on Canada lands, confiscated it without compensation. It was that particular piece of legislation, coupled with the Constitution, which created the fear in those who had money, those who were willing to create businesses and jobs in this country. It created that fear, Mr. Speaker, so investors took their money and left the country. For the balance of their lives they will not trust the leadership of the party which sits opposite the Conservatives in this House. The leader of that party have been supported by the 146 Members on the backbenches, and they have brought fear to this land through that support. They cannot correct the problem, Mr. Speaker, until the Government changes, until we create a new face on economic conditions in this country.
The victims, Mr. Speaker, are the unemployed. Right at this moment, as we speak in this Chamber, in some communities in this country, individual hard-working employees will be getting a letter from the president of their employer. That letter will say that unfortunately economic conditions are such that we have to close this factory, we have to close this mine, lay off 20 per cent of the people, and you are on the list. How many of us in this chamber stop to think how we would feel if that letter arrived on our desk and we had to climb on the subway or on the bus and go home and break the news to our families? How would we feel if we had to tell our families that the income we have been counting on to pay the mortgage on our house, to pay the rent or make car payments has all of a sudden been cut off?
For the average Canadian, Mr. Speaker, there is a sense of betrayal, a sense of bewilderment, because they do not comprehend where and how all this began. Well, Mr. Speaker, it began in the years 1972 to 1974. You can see it in the public accounts of Canada. The Prime Minister was in office, the Hon. John Turner was the Minister of Finance, but the Liberal Party was in a minority position, forced to depend on the New Democratic Party for support. When they look at the financial records of the Government of Canada, people may remember that those were good times. My family taught me that in good times you save a little for a rainy day. That is a sensible way to think about your own future and your own life. In those good times when the Government could have been saving a little for a rainy day, the Liberal Party and the NDP put Canada on the path of borrowing money. We are in good times, so let us go deeper in debt. In those years, Mr. Speaker, federal Government expenditures went up 30 per cent a year. Inflation was around 4 per cent or 5 per cent. And our debt has continued to grow to this day.
When I was elected in 1979, Mr. Speaker, 17 cents out of every federal tax dollar went to pay interest on the national debt. As I stand here three years later, it is over 30 cents. Back in 1979 the Government had 83 cents to spend and 17 cents to pay the interest. Today it is 30 cents on interest and 70 cents

November 5, 1982
Supply
left to provide unemployment insurance benefits, build an airport or try to stimulate the economy. What happens, Mr. Speaker, to individual Canadians if they borrow so much money that everything they earn goes to pay interest? They have nothing left for food. That is what the NDP Party and the Liberal Party did to this country.
As I stand here today, Mr. Speaker, I look with regret on the first seven days of the return of this Parliament. Last spring, one year ago, two years ago, three years ago, we were warning the Government that unemployment was bound to become a flood. We told the Government over and over again that when unemployment rises there are other social costs. Individuals and families are put under stress. And now unemployment has risen to the point where we can expect a 20 per cent increase in the number of Canadians suffering from the problems of alcoholism. We have about 20 per cent more suicides and heart attacks than we had a year ago, all of which are a direct result of the incease in unemployment we have experienced in the past year.
We stood in this House, Mr. Speaker, and asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), if she was planning for that eventuality, what extra money she would provide for it. And we have been told with clarity: "No planning, no extra money. We cannot get it." Well, the reason they cannot get it is that they spent it when times were good. They did not save for a rainy day. Well, the rainy day is here and the Government does not have the money to help Canadians. But the Government bribed Canadians with borrowed money in order to be re-elected, and then the Members opposite have the gall to stand up and say: we do not have the money. But they never tell you why, Mr. Speaker. They do not remind you of the past decade and what they did and the bind they put Canadians in today.
We go to the Minister of Finance and review his public pronouncements in the last couple of weeks. We know there are 1.5 million unemployed Canadians out there and there are an awful lot more Canadians who make less money per hour today than they made a year ago. Incomes are dropping. The average adult person's income in this country has dropped enormously in the past 12 months. People are worried about buying food and about making their house payments. Then, because they are worried, we get the Minister of Finance standing up and going to news conferences and saying, "Now you can worry about your pension and about your family allowance payments. We do not think you are worried enough so we are going to make you worry some more. You do not have enough trouble putting food on your table, so we as a Cabinet are considering cutting out your family allowance payments and pensions". At a time when Canadians are worried enough, why do they do that? What positive value is served by the announcement that the Government is considering these moves, by the announcement: not today but maybe tomorrow? What does this uncertainty do to help this country?
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it does nothing positive but it does a great deal that is negative to increase the distress level, the heart attacks, the suicides, the alcoholism and violence around
us. That is what it does. Yet the 146 Hon. Members opposite continue to support a leadership that does that to the nation at the worst possible time and in the worst possible way. Where is the sanity in that?
In December, 1979 the Progressive Conservative Party, under the leadership of the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) had been in office for nine short months. 1 should like to remind Canadians that in those nine short months the number of employed Canadians increased by 350,000 people- in nine months 350,000 more jobs were created, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who was the Minister of Finance of the day brought in a budget. All across the country learned people judged it to be the fairest budget in the world for the poor. It was the fairest budget for the poor in the decade of the seventies because it gave assistance to a broad range of Canadians and it gave a great deal of assistance to the really poor. At the same time, it encouraged Canadians to own their own home, it gave them the courage to start a small business. Young people dared to dream about owning a farm, or owning a piece of a large business through the stock system.
Built into that budget was the principle of encouraging Canadians to own, to invest and to produce. It encouraged Canadians from coast to coast to create jobs, and in nine months 350,000 jobs were created; that was 40,000 jobs per month, Mr. Speaker. In this last month we have lost 50,000 full-time jobs, Mr. Speaker. A loss of 50,000 jobs and a gain of 40,000 jobs means a difference of 90,000 jobs in a one-month period. That difference was brought about by a change in the attitude of one agency in society, that is, the federal Government.
For the New Democratic Party to put this motion and speak about their compassion for the unemployed is one thing-no one doubts their compassion-but their sanity is a different matter. When we had a government that was creating jobs for Canadians, they threw it out. I hope that the next time Canadians get a chance to vote in this country, they will remember that the New Democratic Party is culpable, is guilty, is a partner in responsibility for 1.5 million people being unemployed in this country today.
That situation exists as a direct consequence of the actions of the man who now leads that Party in the Province of Ontario. He moved the motion. He was the finance critic for that Party, but he did not have the brains to see the wisdom of the budget. He led people down the garden path, and now 1.5 million Canadians are suffering unnecessarily. He was supported in that exercise by the trickery of the leadership of the Party opposite, the Party that does not dare tell the Canadians the truth, the Party that says it does not have any money and tries to bamboozle people about why there is no money. The money is not available because that Party spent it when it should have been saving it. It has chased jobs out of the country through its policies, its attitudes and because of the
November 5, 1982

insane support by backbench Members of that Party for the leadership.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I offer one solution. It will be slow and painful but it will be positive. The solution for the unemployed in this country lies in a federal general election. This recession is the consequence of fear-fear of the leadership of this country. Until the leadership is changed and people Canadians can trust are elected, they will not have a chance and jobs will not be created.
Every day that this Parliament sits, more Canadians will lose their lifetime careers, will be made to depend on the social support system and will risk losing the dignity of being a productive member of society. True patriotism asks simply that seven people walk that 20 feet and start to help this country back to economic health.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in this debate today and make some comments about the unemployment insurance fund. I will offer statistics which I hope will help people understand the impact of the increase in premiums.
Before I do so, however, may I thank the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) for his usual numbing insights into the performance of this Party. The more I listen to him the more I am able to repeat his speech by rote. I am surprised that he did not bring in Ghengis Khan or the Spanish Revolution today, two phenomena that he has managed to discuss in previous monologues. I look forward to hearing about them from that quarter the next time the Hon. Member speaks. I missed that part of his standard address today.

speechtext:
As my colleague points out, he had only 20 minutes so he had to leave something out.
I am pleased to be able to make some comments about the unemployment insurance fund in the presence of the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey). When he assumed the arduous task of changing and strengthening the unemployment insurance fund in the early 1970s, he could not have foreseen how valuable his contribution would be to the fabric of the country in tough times like these. So it is a great pleasure for me to point out that we have been able to draw on the strength of his ideas during this most difficult period.
The unemployment insurance fund is a vital safeguard. It is the first safety net for Canadians when they face the tragedy of unemployment. It was built with the funds of the workers, especially during periods of prosperity, and supported by Government funds, especially in tough times like these.
Every worker knows that the fund is there as a vital insurance plan. He contributes personally to that insurance and he expects responsible Government help and support when the contributions are not sufficient.
In this October statement, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) followed this principle. He strengthened the Government's assistance for the fund and asked those workers who
Supply
have the strength, who have the jobs and the resources, to contribute to the fund as well.
An increase in premiums was brought in on October 27. I should like to put the details of that on the record so that we may understand the consequences of this.
The new rates for 1983 are $2.33 for $100 of insurable earnings for an employee, and $3.22 for $100 of insurable earnings for the employer. The maximum insurable weekly earnings are rising to $385 in 1983. Therefore, the maximum weekly contributions per employee will rise to $8.86 and to $12.40 for the employer. The maximum annual contribution for an employee will rise to $460.72. It will rise to $645.01 for the employer. This is what we are asking ordinary Canadians to contribute to their fund, to their safety net, their insurance policy. At the same time the Government of Canada is contributing $1 billion to pick up the shortfall. At the moment, according to our projections, the fund is running a cumulative deficit of $6.5 billion. It will reach that state by the end of 1983.
If we went only to the insurance aspect of the fund, if we went only to the workers and said, "You must pick up the shortfall", the workers' premium would not be $2.30, it would be $3.75 per $100 of insurable earnings. If we did not go the insurance route, if we simply said that we should subsidize the fund from Government general revenues, then we would have added $3 billion to our deficit in 1983. In both cases, we felt those were too extreme. We felt that the premium increase all the way up to cover the deficit would have been too tough a blow on both the worker and the employer. Equally, as all parties in this House have said, we did not believe that $3 billion could be added on to the federal deficit at this time. So we compromised.
We asked the worker to pay an extra 65 cents a week for every $100 of insurable earnings. We asked the Government to pay $1 billion to soften the total cumulative deficit. What is the impact on the private sector? That is a 39.4 per cent increase in premiums. What is the impact of that on the private sector. In gross terms, the gross revenue is $2,189 million. But we need to remember that for both the worker and the employer, these premiums are tax deductible. We also need to remember that a large portion of the employer related contributions are coming from governments acting as employers.
When we make these calculations, we find that the private sector, in after-tax dollars, is going through a $1,400 million increase, not a $2,100 million increase, roughly two-thirds the gross size. The impact is considerably diminished. Also we need to remember that over the past year some very significant changes have been made in our tax measures.
1 listened with great interest when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) had some comments on the tax rate workers will pay over the coming year. I think he had some of his statistics somewhat wrong. I would like to point

out to him that there have been significant drops in the marginal tax rates. Those drops were increased in the November budget a year ago and are in place now.
We also saw an increase of $50 in the child tax credit for lower- and middle-income families. That increase was introduced in the June budget and it is in effect now. In the October statement, the Minister of Finance continued the tax free status of employer-paid health and dental plans.
These increases in the unemployment insurance plan premiums are not coming in a vacuum, they are coming along with decreases in some of the other taxes that ordinary people are paying.
Most important, and I keep coming back to this, we are following the principle that those who have resources, those who have the funds, those who have the strength, are joining with the Government to extend assistance at this time to those who need help the most.
It is this sense of sharing and compromise, this moderate course, that is typical of the Government's action in the June budget and in the October financial statement. In June, we introduced the six and five program. In that program, by looking at our expenses, by putting them under a magnifying glass, we found $3 billion that we took away from original allocations.
As some of our critics demanded, we could have used that $3 billion simply to reduce the deficit. Had we done so, where would the help be for farmers, fishermen, small-businessmen and the unemployed? Instead, the Government reallocated that money into vital programs for each of those sectors in Canada. In October, we used the same approach. In the October statement we found $1.4 billion that we were able to reallocate into more needy areas, reallocate for jobs and economic stimulation. We should see the October statements as a continuation of the trend started in the June budget, a continuation of the strength that we were able to develop during the initial stages of the six and five program.
We have seen over $4.4 billion reallocated since June into areas that will stimulate jobs and stimulate new economic activity in Canada.
Let us take a look at housing. Housing is a source of quick job creation. Consumers react speedily to this. We found $400 million for housing projects in June, and an additional $165 million in October. New home buyers have been universally praising the Government's $3,000 grant. Existing home owners have been praising the home renovations programs. Not only do people get actual benefit from those programs but, in addition to that, these programs create jobs very quickly.
In small business we have seen the creation of the small business investment grant program in June, and then the extension of the small business bond in October. We saw hundreds of millions of dollars allocated to job creation in June, and then in October the development of the NEED program.
Today in this House we have Bills in front of us to start the special interest subsidy program for farmers and fishermen.
That was a program first started in June. The Government cannot solve each and every one of our problems. We are trying to get that point across to Canadians as hard as we can. The time has come for co-operation in our economy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stressed that point over and over again in his three addresses to the country a short while ago.
The Government cannot solve all our problems, but we can do it together. What the Government is doing during these times is providing some leadership for Canadians. We have done that through the six and five program. Furthermore, the Government can cushion those people who are most in need. I have spoken about how we have reallocated $3 billion in June and an additional $1.4 billion in October. That provides a cushion for those people most in need.
The Government can encourage the economy to begin building and preparing for the day when recovery comes both at home and abroad. We have seen the $500 million that has gone into the NEED program which will help those workers most in need of it. This will also help companies, municipalities and communities across Canada to start on badly needed programs.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is in the House today. He is deeply involved in the rebuilding of the western rail system and the restructuring of the Crow rate so that the railroads can become major instruments for national prosperity over the next decade.
Finally, we have seen the Government stimulate the most sensitive sectors of our economy: housing, small business, forestry, fishing and agriculture. Many extra millions of dollars have been injected in those areas in order to help create jobs.
No one says that the premium increases for the unemployment insurance fund are desirable. We had to take a difficult situation and find a middle of the road course. We could have placed the entire burden on the worker and the employer. It would have been a crippling blow for them. We could have put the whole burden on the deficit, but that would have been an irresponsible move on our part. Instead, we shared and asked those of us who have jobs to contribute something, and then took the resources of the Government and contributed the remainder. That is the type of approach we have taken time and again for job creation and the development of an economic direction to prepare the country for economic recovery.

Mr. Speaker, I am also pleased to take part in this Opposition day debate this afternoon. Since we have had the co-operation of the Government and, I assume, the Official Opposition, as the third NDP speaker I will try not to take up too much time of the House and will keep to my 15 fifteen minutes.
1 was particularly disturbed by the statement of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy)-sometimes called the Minister of unemployment-when he retaliated to
November 5, 1982

the criticism by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper). The Minister's approach is to criticize the person who attacks him and to adopt a defence posture, a stance which is often indefensible. In that manner, he tries to shift the blame for his failures back to the person who criticizes him.
We can cite appalling examples of unemployment program mix-ups and mismanagements which have occurred during the last year, especially over the last six months. This does not suggest that the people who administer unemployment insurance at the local level are incompetent. They have had to carry a tremendous load. This mismanagement suggests that there must be something wrong with the administration of the program in which there are many delays for those wishing to receive premiums. Hence we blame the Minister responsible.
A classic example was provided to me by our research department. It involves the situation in the City of Sudbury where half of the 4,000 claims made by the company- presumably INCO-were in error. Some of the claimants were overpaid, others were underpaid, and many had to wait for five weeks or more. As well, some were cut off entirely from receiving benefits.
While there have been some recent improvements, I would describe the entire program as a bureaucratic nightmare. I hope that the Minister will consider that specific case of Sudbury with quick dispatch. When we criticize the administration or how the Minister handles his role, I think it would behoove him to listen to that criticism, instead of retaliating.
I was here when the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mack-asey) brought in the unemployment insurance scheme. At that time it was considered too generous. At that time we heard much criticism and satirical remarks about the UIC ski team at Banff. They had their own T-shirts, we are told. However, there is no question that in modern society-especially one directed by this Government-unemployment insurance is a necessity.
Yet, I repeat, unemployment insurance delays are awesome. As I said, in Sudbury the delay is six to eight weeks. In Windsor, it is six weeks. There is a six to eight-week delay in Fort McMurray. It is eight weeks in Belleville, eight to ten weeks in Port Alberni and four weeks in Nelson. There is a 12-week delay in Vancouver. I realize that the Minister may find it distasteful for me to cite these examples and that he may find it somewhat nettlesome. He therefore attacks the people who make those criticisms. But these criticisms are made because the people who are facing these delays are average Canadians and they need that money desperately. Many of them are forced to go on welfare. In at least two ridings represented by Members of this Party, the Hon. Members for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) and the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), food distribution centres have been set up in their riding offices. Apparently, they have not only been deluged with serious offers of food but with requests for food from those offices. If that is the state of the nation, it is a most serious situation.
Defensiveness on the part of the Minister is unacceptable. There are all kinds of horror stories which I could list. I would

like to talk about one of those stories because it reflects the prevailing attitude in Canada. This constituent is trying to deal with impatient creditors. His business is one of about 8,000 to 10,000 that officially went bankrupt last year. We do not know how many more just quit. This constituent had to go on to social welfare, but because he had a suite which he was renting out in the basement he could not get full social welfare. He received $420 per month from the Human Resources Department and due to the interest rates he is obligated with a mortgage payment of $938. What will that man do? He is trapped. I am not suggesting that the Human Resources Department in the Province should either ignore his plight or pay the total amount because he is receiving income, but he is still trapped. He will lose his home in the same way he lost his business. This constituent said, "I hope to be back on my feet soon and become a regular part of the working community." I hope so too. He went on to say, "But for the time being I have to swallow my pride and beg for assistance." You see, Mr. Speaker, our culture assumes that if you need help you must be a failure in some way. I wrote back to the man and asked him whether he had paid into unemployment insurance or had paid taxes all his life. He apparently had. I told him, "Well, you have earned that. This is what these programs are all about. This is why they are provided". However, that is not the way people feel about them. People feel very degraded by after exhausting unemployment insurance benefits because they have to seek social assistance. I phoned my riding office today and it reports that the number of people coming into the office who have been forced to go to Human Resources has gone through the ceiling. Most of the people are trying to find other programs because they feel humiliated when they must go on welfare. It is the result of our attitude that somehow if one is poor or needs help, one is a bum. That is known as the lazy bastard theory of social welfare, the feeling that the only people who are obtaining assistance are the socially incompetent. I do not accept that theory and I did not think anyone else should, either.
Other people, notably the UGN, the United Way in my riding, have written to me. They want some money from the community development grants to provide unemployment support centres. Why do we need unemployment support centres? We have human resources offices, unemployment insurance offices and offices of Members of Parliament. We probably even have regional desks so that citizens can reach government. What for? For assistance in job searching, counselling, personal situations, referrals, other facilities, charities and other things. So it is very serious matter in many ridings. Mine is one of the least touched, in the lower mainland, amounting to 11 per cent, because there are a tremendous variety of occupations in my area and we are part of an agricultural and fishing area. We provide a transport corridor. It is a suburban area, and we also have some manufacturing. Many other areas of B.C. are far worse off than mine.

All I know is that it will supposedly produce about one-tenth of the employment we need. However, since the total rail program will supposedly run until 1991 and create 400,000 jobs and he will put in $400 million this year alone, to begin with, and I do not know how many more millions of dollars will be required, I asked the Minister whether he could guarantee that there would be no employment cuts to the railways. The railways have been losing 5,500 jobs a year on an average since 1976. He could not guarantee me that. What concerns me is that all we will do will be to pump more money into the railways for the purposes of upgrading and creating employment, yet we will continue to lose employment. 1 find that hard to understand. I frankly find that to be very confusing because the projections for investment in the railways over the next year have been exactly what they have been over the last two years, that is, $1.3 billion. We are losing employment on the railways at the rate of 5,000 or more jobs each year on the average, since 1976. If the railways do not increase their investment in their own rolling stock, upgrading, track enhancement and improvement, then it will be up to the Government. If the Government is to put in money just to let the railways off the hook, my Party and I think we should have equity. The Minister gets up. Yes, I am suggesting that perhaps we should even nationalize the CNR-

The bottom line is, will it be job-creative or not? If the railways continue to cut their work force, how on earth will that create jobs? The Minister is shaking his head. It is too difficult, too complex for this Member to understand. Therefore, I must be wrong. The money is to be used for tracks and will employ the steel plants, but in the meantime the railways will be nationalized and improved in such a way that they will not need as many people. That is probably what he is suggesting.
The problem with our economic policies and employment strategies is that, first, they have been short-term and, second, they have been wrongheaded. We have been spending all kinds of money to push megaprojects, such as drilling in the Beaufort Sea. What about provinding a few small social welfare bits for Dome Petroleum? That ought to be a good idea, and perhaps a few more, if they really need it. Ignore the guy who will lose his home. Consider Hibernia and the oilsands. The Government will steal from alternative energy sources, from conservation, from the CHIP program and give it to what? Nukes? Will it give money toward stockpiling more heavy water down in Canso or Cape Breton, where there are two plants and $800 million was written off last year? So we have all kinds of money for certain things and not for others. The Nova Scotia Federation of Labour says, "Do it now. Let us start some upgrading and expansion". However, we do not get that. We are asked to pull together. We are asked to do some vague thing called pulling together. We are experiencing business bankruptcies, people are out of work, taxes are rising, but what have we done? The Prime Minister says, "Pull together. We must have unity and co-operation". Who's fault is it? Who has been in the Government for these past 14 years? One cannot blame it all on the municipalities or on world conditions. Hon. Members opposite must bear some of the blame. Today the Prime Minister had the crushing gall to say that he will appoint a former Minister of Finance to tell us
November 5, 1982

what is wrong with our economic policy. That is the height of ludicrousness, if that is a word. He called for us to help him through co-operation to get us out of this mess and said that the way to do it was through six and five.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came into office in 1968 we were second in the world in terms of standard of living. Now we are fourteenth. Some people say that all countries in the western world and in the OECD have problems, but they do not have the unemployment problems that we have. Certainly they do not have the rates of unemployment which we are experiencing. For example, Germany and Japan have half the rate of Canada.
I will tell the House what is wrong with Canada. We are a mega-based, resource-based economy. When a world recession comes along, we have nothing to back it up. We have lost manufacturing jobs by the thousands. I could refer to the list of statistics, but who would want to refer to a list anyway? As a matter of fact, I heard that the level of oratory in the United States Senate fell markedly when people stopped using their emotions and began to quote statistics. Statistics are not good for oratory because no one likes numbers. There are so many big numbers around that no one really listens to them, anyway.
At the present time $100 million is being spent each year on nuclear research and the stockpiling of lethal poisons. Would it not be better to spend it on solar or double-glazed windows? Would it not be better to spend it on things which would create employment at a lot less money per job? 1 think we should. People are going out of business because of cutbacks, but look at the money the Government has taken out of the pockets of people. Naturally businesses will go bankrupt if people are paying most of their money out in interest rates on mortgages. In that event they do not have much left to purchase cars or bicycles; some do not have enough to purchase food. It is not sensible.
We will have five and six on the people but they will not touch oil, which is the prime inflationary factor in Canada today. It will go up again on January 1. I know there is an agreement. I know it will make many people unhappy, but many more people will be unhappy when they have to put away their cars because they have no other option.
They are subsidizing nuclear sales abroad to Mexico. They have subsidized interest rates for Korea or for whatever tin pot dictator comes around wanting to buy one. They will break the contracts with retired public servants. They will allow the dollar to go way down and force many people into bankruptcy. They will scapegoat the Public Service. There will be 800,000 families on welfare by the end of the year; 10,000 more each month. They tell the young that they cannot have jobs. They tell them that they cannot obtain an education by raising the fees. They tell people that they cannot expect to own their own homes. They tell the elderly that they cannot have their indexed pensions because indexing is too expensive and that they must work until they drop.

I say to the Government, as I thank it for allowing me to speak, even if its Members did not listen very much, that it probably has three options.
